chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from al-Kufi from al-Hasan ibn Yusuf from Muhammad ibn Sulayman from Abu Ja'far al-Thani (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, how did it become that when a man accuses his wife, his testimony is 'four oaths by Allah', but if someone else accuses her—a father, brother, son, or relative—he is lashed with the penalty or establishes proof for what he said?' He said, 'Ja'far (peace be upon him) was asked about that, and he said: Indeed, when the husband accuses his wife and says, 'I saw it with my own eyes,' his testimony is 'four oaths by Allah'. And if he says, 'Indeed, I did not see it,' it is said to him, 'Establish proof for what you said,' otherwise he is like the others. And that is because Allah, the Exalted, made for the husband a means of entry that He did not make for others, father or son, which he enters by night and day. So it is permissible for him to say, 'I saw it.' But if someone else says, 'I saw it,' it is said to him, 'What entered you into the place where you see this alone? You are suspected, so it is necessary that the penalty which Allah obligated upon you be established against you.'

key_terms.مَدْخَلًا: A means of entry (referring to the husband's right to enter the marital chamber)

ai.seo_question: Why does a husband's accusation of adultery against his wife not require proof in Shia law?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the jurisprudential rationale behind the husband's exclusive privilege in li'an, distinguishing between a claim of direct visual observation ('I saw it') which requires only four oaths, and a claim of hearsay which demands proof or incurs the hadd penalty. It highlights the concept of 'madkhal' (right of entry) as the basis for this legal asymmetry, a principle deeply rooted in Shia fiqh to balance the husband's unique access to the marital chamber with the need for evidentiary rigor against other relatives.
